clue.text: Chapter (half of it missing) on Miss Pross for example

definitions.note: Miss Pross guards Lucie Manette in Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities

indicators.note: missing tells us a piece is left out of the word Chapter
half of the two-letter word it is just its second letter

explanation.surface: A chapter of a novel, partly lost, about the Dickens character Miss Pross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of it' is T, and 'missing' takes that T out of CHAPTER to leave CHAPER; ON follows. The old spelling without a final E was standard.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss Pross is the devoted companion who escorts and protects the young heroine, a classic example of a female escort.

clue.text: Parting crack -or rather where it ends

explanation.surface: A remark about a split in the hair, or rather the boundary of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The parting suggests hair: a thin crack is a hairline one, and the edge where hair stops growing on the forehead is also so called.
explanation.definitionFit: A very fine split is described by this term; the forehead edge where hair growth stops shares the name.

clue.text: As 'plane needs repair, attempts facetious talk

indicators.note: needs repair shows these letters must be fixed into a fresh order

parts.note: attempts are tries

explanation.surface: As the aircraft needs fixing, some passengers try joking about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needs repair' rearranges AS PLANE to PLEASAN, followed by TRIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Polite jocular remarks and banter exchanged in conversation are this kind of talk.

clue.text: Come back again to harvest fruit

parts.note: to harvest is to reap
a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: Return once more to gather the crop.
explanation.definitionFit: To show up once more after vanishing is to return.

clue.text: A moist-flower is of this genus

definitions.text: A moist-flower is of this genus

parts.words: A moist-flower is of this genus
parts.note: the garden plant called love-in-a-mist belongs to this botanical group, a damp flower name

explanation.surface: Naming the botanical group of a flower associated with mist.
explanation.walkthrough: Love-in-a-mist, a blue cottage-garden flower, is Nigella damascena, so this is its genus.
explanation.definitionFit: Love-in-a-mist is the common name for a species in this genus of the buttercup family.

clue.text: Proportionally represented?

parts.note: looks like electoral reform, but means drawn to size, like a map or model in proportion

explanation.surface: A question about proportional representation in elections.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase suggests proportional representation in voting, but means a drawing or model reduced in exact proportion.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan drawn in fixed ratio to the real thing is one reproduced to size.

clue.text: State service

explanation.surface: A state service, like a government department.
explanation.walkthrough: MASS is the short form for Massachusetts, a US state, and also the Catholic church service.
explanation.definitionFit: Massachusetts is abbreviated this way; the Eucharist in Catholic worship is the church service of the name.

clue.text: Joined forces working like a horse

explanation.surface: Allies who toil as hard as a carthorse.
explanation.walkthrough: Horses harnessed together to pull a cart are yoked as a team, the literal sense behind the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Collaborating partners combined their efforts; a harnessed horse works yoked with others in a team.

clue.text: Better position for a' batsman

explanation.surface: A cricketer would do better if his stance at the wicket improved.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as IN CREASE: the crease is the line a cricket batsman stands at, and being in it keeps him safe from being run out.
explanation.definitionFit: To better something is to make it grow or improve; a batsman standing within the marked line is safe.

clue.text: Are magistrates trained in such arts?

definitions.text: Are magistrates trained in such arts?

parts.words: Are magistrates trained in such arts?
parts.note: magistrates spend their days imposing monetary penalties, so their art is the penalising kind

explanation.surface: A wry question whether the bench has had an art-school education.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the phrase fine arts: magistrates penalise offenders with money, so the arts they practise are the ones named by the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Magistrates punish minor offences with monetary penalties, so the punishing art is this word, as in the phrase fine arts.

clue.text: Harbinger of that which made Isaac reflect

definitions.text: Harbinger of that which made Isaac reflect

parts.words: Harbinger of that which made Isaac reflect
parts.note: Isaac Newton is said to have pondered gravity after a falling fruit; the spring flowering comes before that fruit

explanation.surface: Something heralding whatever set a man named Isaac thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: Isaac is Sir Isaac Newton, whose falling apple supposedly prompted his theory of gravity; the flowers on the tree come before the fruit, so they herald it.
explanation.definitionFit: Spring flowers on the fruit tree precede and so announce the fruit that fell on Newton.

clue.text: "Hell is murky" said Lady Macbeth in this scene

definitions.text: "Hell is murky" said Lady Macbeth in this scene

parts.words: "Hell is murky" said Lady Macbeth in this scene
parts.note: Lady Macbeth speaks the line while wandering at night, unconscious, in Act V of Shakespeare's play

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's Macbeth asking which scene it comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act V of Macbeth, Lady Macbeth walks in her slumber, rubbing her hands and muttering lines like this one.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Macbeth's famous Act V scene shows her wandering in her slumber, confessing guilt.

clue.text: Silver in Slough? Appearance is illusory

indicators.note: in places the symbol for silver inside the word for a slough

parts.note: a slough is a bog or swamp, so mire
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A remark that the silver one spots in a swamp is only an illusion.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the town west of London, but it is the common noun for a bog. 'in' puts AG inside MIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A desert vision of water is the textbook appearance that proves to be illusory.

clue.text: Like fire-engines with run of hose

explanation.surface: Describing fire-engines and the hoses they unreel.
explanation.walkthrough: Hose here is stockings, not fire hose: a run in a stocking is a ladder in British English.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire-engines carry extendable climbing frames; stockings with a vertical run are said to have ladders.

clue.text: New Street's maker 'of canopies

indicators.note: new suggests the letters of the word are made fresh in a different order

parts.note: the word with its possessive s counted as a letter

explanation.surface: A craftsman on New Street who makes canopies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' looks like part of a street name, but it is the anagram signal for STREETS; 'maker of' just links the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tester is a canopy over a four-poster bed or pulpit, so the plural names several of them.

clue.text: Composed of right and left quaint arrangement

indicators.note: arrangement says the letters are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: Something made of right and left in a quaint pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' looks like 'made up of', but it is the definition, calm; 'arrangement' rearranges R, L and QUAINT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone composed is calm and serene, unruffled by events.

clue.text: Eldest son heard to question item dealing with inflation

indicators.note: heard tells us to take the word for an eldest son by its sound

parts.note: the eldest son is traditionally the heir
to pump someone is to question them persistently

explanation.surface: A firstborn reported grilling someone about the cost of living.
explanation.walkthrough: HEIR sounds like AIR; to pump a person is to grill them for information. Inflation means blowing up tyres, not rising prices.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand or foot device for forcing gas into tyres and balls is the tool for blowing them up.

clue.text: Trains do go out underneath the arch

indicators.note: go out suggests the letters break ranks and take a different order

explanation.surface: Trains run out from under a railway arch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go out' rearranges TRAINS DO.
explanation.definitionFit: In architecture the inner curved underside of an arch has this technical name.

clue.text: One article' in official record gives the petty details

indicators.note: in places one item inside the other, here the numeral and article inside the record

parts.note: the minutes are the official record of a meeting
I is the Roman numeral for one
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: One item in the minutes of a meeting covers the small print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts IA inside MINUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny trivial points or particulars are called by this Latin plural.

clue.text: Blow struck for beauty

explanation.surface: A punch landed to win a beauty contest.
explanation.definitionFit: A knockout punch leaves someone dazed; a strikingly attractive person is a knockout too.

clue.text: .Chance finding of a small volume, single impression

parts.note: cc is cubic centimetres, a small volume measure
I is the Roman numeral for one, so single
a dent is an impression made by a blow

explanation.surface: A lucky find of a slim book, one printing only.
explanation.walkthrough: Volume and impression look like book terms here, but they mean CC (cubic centimetres) and a dent.
explanation.definitionFit: A mishap or stroke of luck is something that happens by chance, unplanned.

clue.text: Bridge-player not forbidden to call out

parts.note: East is one of the four players at the bridge table, abbreviated E
licit means lawful, not forbidden

explanation.surface: A card player allowed to make a bid.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge the four players are North, South, East and West, so one player gives E. 'call' also suggests a bridge bid.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw out a response or reaction from someone is to evoke it.

clue.text: Schools appearing to be for: those going places

explanation.surface: Schools that look set for anyone travelling.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to coach them; railway carriages pulled by locomotives are what travellers ride.

clue.text: Ask Tapley the sequel to the written enquiry

definitions.text: the sequel to the written enquiry

parts.note: to ask is to question
Mark Tapley is the cheerful servant in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit

explanation.surface: An instruction to put a follow-up query to someone called Tapley.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Tapley is a Dickens character from Martin Chuzzlewit; his first name follows the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: In writing, a query is followed by the hooked punctuation sign that ends it.

clue.text: One test out of a thousand

parts.note: ex means out of, as in ex-directory
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: A single test that only one in a thousand passes.
explanation.definitionFit: A school or university assessment of knowledge is a single such paper.

clue.text: In assembly one twice gets the bird

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
bis is Latin for twice, used in music and on encores

explanation.surface: Someone at a meeting twice gets jeered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets the bird' sounds like being booed, but bird is the definition. In assembly just joins one and twice together.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-billed wading species sacred in ancient Egypt is a bird.

clue.text: In part of play note on keeping still

indicators.note: on means the note is set after the rest in this down-the-page order

parts.note: Act IV is a part of a play
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: Actors told during one scene to hold a pose.
explanation.walkthrough: ACT IV is the fourth part of a play; the musical note E comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone or something motionless, not moving or doing anything, is idle.

clue.text: Gave up — what George did about son

indicators.note: about tells us the ruling word goes round the abbreviation for son

parts.note: a King George ruled, so he reigned

explanation.surface: Quit, like a father's behaviour concerning his boy.
explanation.walkthrough: George is a king of Britain, so what he did was rule; 'about' puts S inside REIGNED.
explanation.definitionFit: To quit a post or give in to fate is to step down or accept it.
